claims.text: In as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films, magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are primarily governed by microstructural and interfacial effects controlling magnetostructural-transition nucleation and growth.
The starting FeMnNiGeSi-type films have an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The starting films can be produced by magnetron sputtering.
Reducing film thickness increases the film's surface-to-volume ratio.
Film thickness affects the density and distribution of interfaces relevant to the magnetostructural transition.
Interfaces in these films serve as nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Increasing the interfacial contribution by reducing thickness lowers the transition's nucleation-energy barrier.
Lowering the nucleation barrier produces a more gradual and broader magnetocaloric transition.
Lowering the nucleation barrier diminishes hysteresis relative to thicker films or bulk forms.
Volumetric effects dominate the transition behavior of thicker films and bulk forms.
FeMnNiGeSi-type films below roughly 1 micrometer will have a broader magnetocaloric transition than the thicker-film baseline.
FeMnNiGeSi-type films below roughly 1 micrometer will have lower hysteretic losses than the thicker-film baseline.
Thinner FeMnNiGeSi-type films will provide improved heat-exchange performance.
Thicker as-deposited films, bulk ingots, or melt-spun microribbons provide a baseline with a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition and significant hysteresis.
Holding composition and deposition conditions constant while varying thickness is intended to isolate thickness as the experimental variable.
Processing conditions can affect phase or compositional stability in high-entropy alloys.
The interface-controlled regime is likely to occur below approximately 1 micrometer.
Other microstructural or compositional instabilities may override the proposed thickness dependence.
The threshold thickness may depend on processing-induced defects.
A lack of transition broadening and hysteresis reduction upon reducing thickness would falsify the proposed surface-to-volume-controlled nucleation mechanism.
